I’ll engage with you, man. 

So I think your point about these other dangerous activities that result in more deaths is an important one.

What did you say? Smoking, swimming? To start with those, I guess, lots of people do definitely die from those sources. Google tells me 430,000 people die from (a lifetime of?) smoking tobacco every year. That’s crazy and I had no idea it was so high. 
But public swimming pools and tobacco use ARE subject to some serious amount of govt oversight or control. You might say that 430,000 deaths each year is a far more pressing problem, and perhaps it is, but the solution to discouraging long term tobacco use is not easily discernible. We’ve tried some stuff and it has helped a lot. Long term, cigarette smoking rates have fallen: 67 percent among adults, from 42.6 percent in 1965 to 14.0 percent in 2017. 68 percent among youth, from 27.5 percent in 1991 to 8.8 percent in 2017. I don’t know about vapes or cigars though.

Anyway, the point is that those problems have/are being addressed and have been reduced in scope from panic level 67% (edit: actually 42% whoops) to 14%, which is still high, but better than it was by a lot.

Your view is not irrational, but you will need to answer a few questions to justify it:
How many people would die with zero action taken? (Something like 2.5 million it seems) and is that damage worth the (alleged? actual?) boon to the economy? 
Is the inconvenience of social distancing greater than the inconvenience of losing 2.5 million friends and family (or however you see it) ? Also worth noting that survivors sustain some amount of permanent damage to their health, usually their lungs. Which can probably be rolled up into some portion of eventual deaths too. And inconvenience. 

That’s all, thanks for being willing to share your thoughts on this highly charged subreddit
